subsection: 9. Case study: Robert Owen's model village at New Lanark

notes.h: Why a model village was needed: early cotton mills and laissez-faire
notes.b: Owen's experiment only makes sense against the background of the early factory system, which grew out of industrialisation (the shift from hand work at home to machine production in factories). New Lanark stood out because almost every other mill owner worked in the opposite way.
points: Early cotton mills were water-powered spinning mills, where workers put in very long hours, children did much of the work, and discipline relied on fines and beatings.

Water-powered mills had to stand where there was falling water, far from towns, so owners had to build housing and bring in workers. This is why a mill and a village went together, and why many rural mills took pauper apprentices (workhouse children bound to the mill owner).
The dominant view was laissez-faire (the belief that the state should not interfere in the economy), so most employers and politicians thought the state should not regulate wages or hours.
Because of laissez-faire, Owen's ideas and his call for a factory law were unusual.
notes.tip: Document and paragraph questions ask why New Lanark was different from other mills. Contrast it with the usual long hours, child labour and punishment.

notes.h: Owen's background and the Chorlton mills
notes.b: Robert Owen was a Welsh-born manager who learned the cotton trade in Manchester before taking charge of a much larger mill complex in Scotland. His early life gave him both the skills and the ideas he later used at New Lanark.
points: Robert Owen was born in 1771 at Newtown, Montgomeryshire, Wales. He left school at about ten and worked for drapers (cloth merchants) in Stamford, London and Manchester.

By about twenty, in the early 1790s, he was managing a large cotton-spinning mill in Manchester owned by Peter Drinkwater. Later in the 1790s he became a partner in the Chorlton Twist Company, Manchester.
His Manchester years showed him how mill workers and their families lived, which shaped his belief that people are formed by their surroundings.

His central idea was that character is formed for the individual, not by the individual, through circumstances and education. This is why every reform at New Lanark aimed at changing the environment, because he thought changing the environment would change the people.
The environmentalist ideas of Enlightenment thinkers, who held that character is formed by surroundings, shaped his outlook.
In 1799 he married Caroline Dale, daughter of David Dale, the Glasgow merchant who owned the New Lanark mills, which gave him a family connection to Dale and to the mills.
In the same year, 1799, Owen and his Manchester partners bought New Lanark from Dale. Owen took over as manager on 1 January 1800, aged 28.
notes.tip: Be ready to state Owen's central idea in one sentence: character is formed by circumstances, so improve the environment and you improve the people. It explains every reform he made.

notes.h: New Lanark before Owen: the site, David Dale and the people
notes.b: New Lanark was already a very large mill community when Owen arrived. Knowing who built it, and how its workers were housed, shows what Owen inherited and what he changed.
points: New Lanark stands on the River Clyde near Lanark, Scotland. It was founded in the mid-1780s (building began in 1785) by David Dale, at first with Richard Arkwright, the cotton pioneer, who soon withdrew.
The mills used water power from the Falls of Clyde, which was the reason Dale chose the site, and the cotton-spinning works were among the largest in Britain.

David Dale was a Glasgow merchant and banker and was thought a comparatively humane employer. He housed the pauper children in dormitories, fed them and provided evening schooling, but the children still worked long days.
In 1800 about 2,000 people lived at New Lanark, including about 500 pauper children from the poorhouses of Edinburgh and Glasgow.
Do not mix up the three men: Dale was the founder and Owen's father-in-law, Arkwright was an early partner and inventor of the water frame, and Owen was manager from 1800 and then part-owner.
notes.tip: Keep Dale, Arkwright and Owen apart in your answers. Dale founded the mills, Arkwright was only an early partner, and Owen was manager from 1800.

notes.b: When Owen arrived he found a hard-working but troubled community. Much of this picture comes from Owen's own writings, so it is his account and not neutral evidence.
points: The mill day was about thirteen hours including meal breaks, and children as young as about six worked in the mills and then attended evening classes, when they were tired.
By Owen's account, the village houses were dirty and overcrowded, the streets were filthy and sanitation (drains, waste removal and clean water) was poor.
Owen described the workforce as marked by drunkenness, theft and disorder, and the people distrusted a manager from outside.
Owen said that discipline relied on fines and physical punishment, and he set out to replace it.
He saw these conditions as the result of environment rather than of individual wickedness, so he set out to change the environment in order to change character.
Owen later argued that the conditions at New Lanark reflected the wider failings of the factory system rather than the particular fault of its managers.
notes.tip: Remember that the thirteen-hour day includes meal breaks, so do not compare it directly with the later figure for hours of actual work. Remember too that this picture is Owen's own account.

notes.h: Owen's reforms in the mill: child labour, hours and wages
notes.b: Owen believed that humane treatment would pay for itself, so his first reforms changed the terms of work in the mill. Each one targeted a way the old system harmed workers, especially children.
points: Owen stopped taking pauper apprentices, which ended the supply of workhouse children, and raised the minimum working age, so that by 1816 no child under ten worked in the mills. Younger children went to school instead, and the change was gradual.
He cut the working day, so that by 1816 it was under eleven hours of actual work (about ten and a half hours), and he argued that output did not fall.
During an American embargo on cotton exports the mills stood idle. Owen paid wages to the idle workers for about four months, which won their trust and loyalty.
He used profits to pay for schools and welfare, which he treated as a sound investment in the workforce, because he expected better-treated workers to produce better work.
notes.tip: Use specific dated facts: Owen took over in 1800, and by 1816 no child under ten worked in the mills. Write the working day as under eleven hours of actual work, not an exact figure.

notes.h: Discipline without beating: the silent monitor
notes.b: Owen did not want to run the mill by fines and blows, so he looked for a way to encourage good conduct through reward and example. His best-known device was the silent monitor.
points: Physical punishment ended at New Lanark, and Owen replaced it with a system of reward and example.
The silent monitor was a four-sided block of wood hung beside each worker. Each side was a colour: black (bad conduct), blue (indifferent), yellow (good) and white (excellent).
The superintendent turned the block each day to show the previous day's conduct, and conduct was also recorded in books of character.
Owen used it so that behaviour was recorded without shouting or beating. Pride in a good colour and shame at a bad one were the motives, so that workers wanted to improve.
notes.tip: If asked how the silent monitor worked, give the four colours in order from bad to excellent, say who turned it and when, and explain the aim: no shouting or beating, shame and pride instead.

notes.h: Reforms in the village: housing, store and sick fund
notes.b: Owen believed that a worker's home and daily life shaped character as much as the mill did, so he reformed the village as well as the work.
points: Owen improved and repaired the village housing, had the streets cleaned and rubbish collected, and encouraged households to keep their homes clean and to live in an orderly way.
The village store sold good-quality goods at little more than cost. It made a small profit, which helped to pay for the schools.
The sale of spirits was controlled, which was meant to reduce the drunkenness Owen had found.
A sick fund, to which workers contributed part of their wages, gave help in illness, so a sick worker was not left without support.
notes.tip: Say that the store sold goods at little more than cost, and that its small profit helped fund the school. Do not say it sold goods at cost.

notes.h: Schools and the Institute for the Formation of Character
notes.b: Owen thought education was the strongest way to form character, so he made schooling the heart of New Lanark. The schools were housed in a new building, the Institute for the Formation of Character.
points: The Institute for the Formation of Character opened on 1 January 1816. By day it housed the infant school and children's classes, and in the evening it was used for classes, lectures, music and dancing for older children and adults.

The infant school (1816) took children from about one, as soon as they could walk, to six. It was often described as the first infant school in Britain, and its teacher was James Buchanan, who later ran an infant school in London.

In the infant school children were taught by kindness, through play, songs, dancing, pictures, maps and natural objects rather than books and rote learning (learning by repetition), and there was no punishment.
A day school took children of about six to ten, and evening classes for older children and young workers taught reading, writing, arithmetic, singing, dancing and geography.

Owen kept religious teaching out as far as he could, because he disliked organised religion. His partners, including the Quaker William Allen, opposed this and objected to the dancing and music, and the clergy also criticised it.
The infant school attracted visitors from abroad.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the three parts: the Institute is the building (1816), the infant school was inside it, and the day school was for older children. For document questions, recognise kindness, no punishment, pictures, maps, objects, singing and dancing.

notes.b: Owen's schemes cost money, so they needed backers who would accept them. His partnerships show how far his reforms were supported, and why they were also limited.
points: The mills stayed profitable under Owen, so he used it as proof that humane treatment and profit could go together.
His earlier partners objected to spending profits on schools, and the dispute ended with the mills sold at auction in 1813.

The new partnership of 1813 included the philosopher Jeremy Bentham and the Quaker William Allen. They agreed to take a fixed 5 per cent return on their capital, with the rest of the profit going to benefit the community.
Allen and other partners objected to the dancing, drill and lack of religious teaching in the schools, and to Owen's attacks on religion.
In the 1820s the partners imposed changes, which helped to push Owen out.
notes.tip: Quick dated facts score well: the 1813 partners and their 5 per cent return, and the disputes over religion that led to changes in the 1820s.

notes.h: Owen's writings and the campaign for factory legislation
notes.b: Owen did not keep his ideas to New Lanark. He wrote about them and pressed Parliament to pass a law, which put him ahead of most employers.
points: A New View of Society, or Essays on the Formation of the Human Character, was four essays published in 1813-14. In it Owen argued that character is formed by circumstances and that society could improve its people by improving conditions and education.

The state had already begun to act. The Health and Morals of Apprentices Act of 1802, promoted by Sir Robert Peel the elder (a cotton manufacturer and father of the Prime Minister), limited the hours of pauper apprentices.
From 1815 Owen campaigned for a factory law, and in 1816 he gave evidence to a select committee (a group of MPs investigating a subject) chaired by the elder Peel.
The Cotton Mills and Factories Act of 1819 allowed no children under nine in cotton mills and limited children aged nine to sixteen to twelve hours a day.
The Act was weaker than Owen wanted. It was enforced by local magistrates with no inspectors, so it was poorly enforced.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the 1802 Act (pauper apprentices, the elder Peel) with the 1819 Act (all children in cotton mills, after Owen's campaign) or later Factory Acts.

notes.h: Villages of co-operation and the attack on religion
notes.b: Owen's ambitions grew from one mill village to a plan for self-supporting villages of co-operation. In 1817 he also made a public move that cost him much support.
points: In 1817 Owen presented a plan for villages of co-operation (self-supporting co-operative communities for the unemployed poor) to a committee for the relief of the manufacturing poor in London. In 1820 he set out a similar plan in a Report to the County of Lanark.
William Cobbett, a radical who saw such villages as a way of controlling the poor, mocked them as "parallelograms of paupers".
In August 1817, at a public meeting in London, Owen denounced all organised religions. This lost him much support among the respectable and powerful.
notes.tip: Keep apart New Lanark (a reformed mill village that worked), New Harmony (a co-operative community that failed) and the villages of co-operation (never built as Owen planned).

notes.h: After New Lanark: New Harmony and Owen's departure
notes.b: Owen next tried to build a fully co-operative community. His absence and these experiments ended his direct involvement at New Lanark.
points: Owen went to the United States in 1824. In 1825 he bought Harmony, Indiana, from the Rappites (a German religious community) and founded New Harmony, a co-operative experiment.
Quarrels among the members and poor organisation brought New Harmony to a breakdown within about two years, and Owen left in 1827.
Other Owenite communities in Britain also failed: Orbiston, near Motherwell, Scotland (1825-27), and Queenwood, Hampshire (1839-45).
Owen gave up his interest in New Lanark in 1828-29. The mills carried on under others and spun cotton until 1968, and New Lanark remained a reference point for later social reformers.
notes.tip: Say that New Harmony was founded in 1825 and Owen left in 1827 when it broke down. Give the New Lanark departure as 1828-29 or by 1829, not a single exact year.

notes.h: Co-operation and socialism: the Labour Exchange, the GNCTU and Rochdale
notes.b: Owen's ideas moved from mill reform to a wider vision of society based on co-operation. Socialism, as Owen used it, meant common ownership and co-operation instead of competition.
points: The National Equitable Labour Exchange, set up in London in 1832, exchanged goods for labour notes (paper money based on hours of work). It collapsed in 1834.
The Grand National Consolidated Trades Union of 1834 aimed at one great union of all workers and a co-operative society. Owen was its inspiration and best-known figure rather than its formal leader.
The union collapsed later in 1834 after employers' lock-outs (refusing to let workers in) and the Tolpuddle case. Owen's journal of 1834 was called The New Moral World.

Owen's ideas inspired co-operative societies. The Rochdale Pioneers in Lancashire opened a co-operative store in 1844, which began the lasting consumer co-operative movement, although Owen did not found it.
Owen's followers, the Owenites, were among the first in Britain to be called socialists, in the late 1820s and 1830s.
Marx and Engels later called Owen a utopian socialist, meaning that he hoped to change society by example and persuasion rather than class struggle. Owen died at Newtown in 1858.
notes.tip: Keep the three dates apart: Labour Exchange 1832, GNCTU 1834 and Rochdale Pioneers 1844. Remember that Owen did not found the Rochdale Pioneers.

notes.h: Why the model was not widely copied
notes.b: Few owners copied New Lanark, even though it was profitable and famous. Examiners want several distinct reasons, so each one is worth learning.
points: Other owners thought welfare too costly in a competitive industry, and believed that their profits depended on low wages and long hours.
Laissez-faire beliefs also told owners and politicians not to interfere with how a business treated its workers.
New Lanark's success depended on Owen's personal control and on unusual partners, which few owners were willing to accept.
Urban steam-powered mills did not need to house their workers, because workers lived in the town, so they had no reason to build villages.
Because Owen attacked religion and promoted socialism, he discredited his example, and his larger schemes, New Harmony and the Labour Exchange, failed.

Some ideas were partly copied. Later employers built model villages, such as Saltaire in Yorkshire (Titus Salt's village, whose mill opened in 1853), but these were paternalist (the owner in charge) rather than co-operative, and infant schools spread.
notes.tip: A 100-mark essay on why New Lanark was not generally adopted needs several distinct reasons: cost and competition, laissez-faire, dependence on Owen, his religious views, the failure of his later schemes, and rural versus urban mills.

notes.b: Opinion of Owen was divided in his own lifetime and has stayed divided among historians. Both sides need evidence.
points: Admirers: thousands of visitors came to New Lanark in the late 1810s and 1820s, including reformers, churchmen and royalty such as the future Tsar Nicholas I of Russia.

Critics: employers who thought him a dangerous dreamer, churchmen and his own partners offended by his views on religion, and radicals such as Cobbett who saw his villages as a way of controlling the poor.
Later views: historians see him as a pioneer of industrial welfare, infant education, factory reform and co-operation, often called the father of British socialism and of the co-operative movement.
But he can also be seen as paternalist, because New Lanark depended on supervision and control (the silent monitor, house inspections) by one man.
New Lanark became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001.
notes.tip: Use the pairs when judging him: pioneer versus paternalist, and contemporary praise versus contemporary criticism.

notes.h: Assessment: New Lanark and Owen's influence
notes.b: Judging Owen means setting what New Lanark achieved against what limited it, and then asking how far his wider influence reached.
points: Achievement: New Lanark combined shorter hours, no young child labour, schools and a decent village with profit.
Limit: it was one village, it depended on Owen, and his partners curbed it.
Achievement of his wider influence: he helped bring about the 1819 Act, the infant school movement and co-operation.
Limit of his wider influence: the 1819 Act was weak, and New Harmony, the Labour Exchange and the GNCTU failed.
Contemporary view: friends saw a benevolent experiment, while critics saw a paternalist whose religious views were dangerous.
Later view: historians see a pioneer of industrial welfare, though one whose methods of control were paternalistic.
Compared with Robert Peel the Prime Minister, who changed national law, Owen worked by example outside government, so his influence stayed local.
A good verdict weighs both sides: a local success and a pioneer of ideas, but not a model that changed the system.
notes.tip: Pair each achievement with a limit and end with a clear verdict. In comparisons with Peel, say that Peel changed national law while Owen's example stayed local.

keyTerms.definition: The principle of people working together and sharing benefits, which Owen promoted at New Lanark and in later co-operative schemes.
Owen's wooden block with a different colour on each side, turned to show a worker's conduct, used instead of punishment at New Lanark.

keyTerms.term: Institute for the Formation of Character
keyTerms.definition: The meeting hall and school opened at New Lanark in 1816 to provide adult education, music, dancing and lectures.
The school opened at New Lanark in 1816 for young children, which used games, songs and practical activities rather than rote learning.
A planned community built by an employer to improve the housing, health, education and conduct of its workforce.
The Act that barred children under nine from cotton mills and limited the working hours of older children, a result of Owen's campaigning.
Owen's essays of 1813–1816 arguing that human character is formed by circumstances and that society should improve them.
The co-operative community founded by Owen in Indiana in 1825, which failed within a few years.

factCards.definition: In 1816 Owen stopped employing children under ten in the New Lanark mill.
The village store at New Lanark sold goods at cost price, so that workers did not pay a shopkeeper's profit.
Owen bought the Harmony settlement in Indiana in 1825 and founded New Harmony as a co-operative community.
The Lancashire co-operative store set up in 1844 that became a model for the later co-operative movement.
New Lanark was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001 for its importance to industrial social reform.
Robert Owen was born in Newtown in 1771, worked in Manchester cotton mills and became manager of New Lanark in January 1800.

factCards.term: Owen's marriage and connection to Dale
factCards.definition: Owen married Caroline Dale, daughter of David Dale, who sold the New Lanark mills to the Chorlton partners in 1799.
The New Lanark mills on the River Clyde were founded in 1785 by David Dale with Richard Arkwright, using water power from the Falls of Clyde.
In 1813 Owen's new backers included Jeremy Bentham and the Quaker William Allen, who accepted a fixed return and later objected to some of his schemes.
Owen sailed for America in 1824 and ended his connection with New Lanark in about 1829, after disputes with his partners.
By 1816 Owen had cut the working day to ten and three-quarter hours, with no children under ten in the mills.
After Owen's campaign the Cotton Mills and Factories Act of 1819 barred children under nine and limited hours for older children, but had no inspectors.
